--- title: "[Graph.trav_reverse_edge()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Traverse to reverse edges. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L17098-L17178){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.trav_reverse_edge(add_to_selection=False) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Traverse to reverse edges](/assets/graphs/trav-reverse-edge.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: two edges are selected in the accent color, C to D and A to C; C and D are also joined by a second edge from D back to C. Right: after trav_reverse_edge() only D to C is selected, the reverse of C to D; A to C has no reverse edge, so it contributes nothing." width="100%"} From the currently selected edges, finds the reverse edges. For each selected edge `A->B`, every edge `B->A` in the graph is collected (so parallel reverse edges are all picked up). Selected edges that have no reverse counterpart contribute nothing. The node selection is not touched. This is useful for: - finding reciprocated relationships (mutual follows, two-way trade flows, replies) - checking whether a set of directed links is answered in the other direction - expanding a selection of one-way edges to include their return paths The method is intended for directed graphs. It does not check directedness, but in an undirected graph a single edge is not its own reverse, so the selection is usually emptied unless the same pair was added twice with swapped endpoints. If no edges are selected, nothing happens. Each selected edge is matched by scanning the edge list, so the cost grows with (selected edges x total edges). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [add_to_selection]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Controls what happens to the edges that were selected before the call. If `False` (the default), the edge selection is replaced by the reverse edges only, so edges without a reverse drop out. If `True`, the reverse edges are added to the existing edge selection, leaving the original edges selected as well. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this small follower network, Ann and Bob follow each other while Cat's follow of Ann is one-way. With `add_to_selection=False` (the default), selecting the two edges that leave Ann and Cat and traversing leaves only `Bob->Ann` selected, since `Cat->Ann` has no reverse (in the exported table, Ann is node `1` and Bob is node `2`): ::: {#fadf5cf6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["Ann", "Bob", "Cat"]) .add_edges([("Ann", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Ann"), ("Cat", "Ann")]) ) ann_to_bob = graph.find_edge_ids(source="Ann", target="Bob") cat_to_ann = graph.find_edge_ids(source="Cat", target="Ann") graph.select_edges_by_id(ann_to_bob + cat_to_ann) graph.trav_reverse_edge() graph.get_edge_df_ws() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
